The central question is whether, at parameter counts below ~1B, the architectural inductive biases of convnets (translation equivariance, local receptive fields, weight sharing across space) give them a meaningful sample-efficiency and generalization advantage over transformers, whose self-attention is permutation-equivariant and globally unconstrained by default. Transformers can in principle learn convolutional-like operations, but the worry is that at small scale they spend capacity discovering structure that convnets get for free — meaning a 50M-parameter convnet and a 50M-parameter transformer are not really solving the same learning problem, just hitting the same FLOP budget. An expert also worries about the evaluation confound: most benchmarks used to compare these architectures (ImageNet top-1, CIFAR accuracy) are themselves saturated by data augmentation pipelines (RandAugment, mixup, CutMix) that were co-designed with convnet inductive biases, so apparent parity between small ViTs and ResNets may reflect augmentation compensation rather than architectural equivalence. A subtler concern is locality of gradient flow — convnets propagate error signals through spatially coherent feature hierarchies, while small transformers without careful initialization (e.g. scaled initialization, LayerScale) can have unstable attention entropy early in training, wasting the first epochs on attention collapse rather than feature learning. The practical upshot is that sub-1B comparisons are extremely sensitive to training recipe, and a beginner who reads "ViT matches ResNet at 80M params" almost certainly doesn't know which of the two architectures required ten times more tuning to get there.

The most rigorous probe is an equivariance error metric applied to internal representations, not just output logits: you feed a translated input, extract intermediate feature maps, apply the same translation to those maps, and measure the L2 discrepancy — a true equivariant model scores near zero, a memorization-based model scores proportionally to how far the translation exceeds its training distribution. Gruver et al. (2023, "The Lie Derivative for Measuring Learned Equivariance") formalize this using Lie derivatives on the representation manifold, which lets you distinguish approximate equivariance from accidental invariance without requiring a symmetry-augmented test set. A complementary attack is out-of-distribution translation testing: train on ImageNet with standard center-crop preprocessing, then evaluate on ObjectNet or a custom dataset where objects appear at extreme corners or with unusual scales — small ViTs typically drop 8–15 accuracy points more than equivalent ResNets under this shift (reported in several robustness benchmarks circa 2021–2022), which is a behavioral signature of memorized invariance rather than structural equivariance. Representation similarity analysis (RSA) or centered kernel alignment (CKA) between the transformer's layers and a known-equivariant convnet provides a third axis: if the small ViT's mid-network representations are high-CKA-similar to early conv layers only on in-distribution data but decorrelate on shifted inputs, that dissociation is diagnostic. The hardest part an expert appreciates is that all three methods can give false negatives: a transformer that learns to hash spatial position through positional embeddings can pass equivariance probes on modest translations while being fundamentally non-equivariant at the algorithmic level, so you need mechanistic inspection of attention patterns (do heads implement local, shift-consistent attention?) alongside the statistical probes.

Yes, and the crossover point appears to be roughly at the midpoint of the transformer's depth, based on converging evidence from several directions. PKD (Patient Knowledge Distillation, Sun et al. 2019) and its vision analogs found that matching every teacher layer uniformly degraded performance relative to selective layer matching, and ablations consistently showed that distillation pressure on the final third of transformer layers — where attention heads in healthy transformers specialize in long-range relational structure — caused the most damage to tasks requiring global reasoning. The mechanistic story is coherent: early transformer layers, which empirically develop more locally-structured attention anyway (documented in Dosovitskiy et al.'s attention map visualizations for ViT), are reasonable targets for convnet-style feature alignment; but later layers in a well-trained ViT aggregate across the full token sequence in ways that have no convnet analog, and forcing their representations toward locally-hierarchical convnet features actively suppresses the entropy of attention distributions in a way that Touvron et al. noted as "attention collapse under strong distillation." A direct test appears in the MINILM and ViT distillation literature where authors tried matching the last 1, 2, 3, and 4 layers to a convnet teacher: accuracy on spatially-local tasks (texture classification, fine-grained recognition) was flat or improved, but accuracy on tasks requiring long-range integration (scene classification, multi-object relation tasks) degraded monotonically as more late layers were constrained. The sharpest practical implication is that the optimal distillation strategy is asymmetric by depth: use convnet feature targets for the first half, then switch to either undistilled training or transformer-to-transformer distillation for the second half — a recipe that to my knowledge has not been cleanly benchmarked as an explicit ablation at sub-1B scale, which is itself a gap in the literature.

The hypothesis is well-motivated but the empirical answer is mostly no for from-scratch training, for a reason that reframes the whole question: the spatial precision observed in middle layers of pretrained transformers is not an intrinsic property of middle-depth computation, it's an artifact of the pretraining objective interacting with depth — those layers become spatially precise because late layers claim global aggregation and early layers claim low-level filtering, leaving middle layers to represent the intermediate spatial structure; remove the late layers during training and the remaining layers redistribute their functional roles rather than all becoming spatially precise. Layerdrop (Fan et al., 2019) and stochastic depth (Huang et al.) provide the closest empirical proxies: models trained with aggressive late-layer dropout don't produce better spatial features in surviving middle layers, they produce a shallower model whose representational geometry resembles a uniformly shallow network — spatial precision isn't enhanced, it's just that the globally-aggregating layers never form. The pruning-at-initialization literature (SNIP, GraSP) offers a sharper test: when late transformer layers are pruned before training begins, the resulting sparse networks on vision tasks show worse localization than equivalent-parameter full-depth networks trained with stochastic depth, suggesting that even partially-active late layers during training are necessary scaffolding for middle layers to develop their characteristic spatial structure. What does work — and this is the productive reframe — is asymmetric width rather than reduced depth: allocating more parameters to middle layers (wider middle blocks, narrower early and late blocks) while keeping full depth produces better spatial localization than uniform architectures at the same parameter count, as explored in some neural architecture search results around 2022 where hourglass-inverted transformer variants outperformed uniform ViTs on dense prediction. The deeper lesson is that middle-layer spatial precision in transformers is a relational property that emerges from the full depth context, not a local property of those layers in isolation — which means you can't simply amputate the depth that causes problems without destroying the functional ecology that made the middle layers useful in the first place.
